textbookText: with each plane hosting four satellites. These satellites orbit at an altitude of about 20,000 km above the Earth at a speed of 14,000 km/h. To determine a location on the Earth’s surface, GPS requires signals from three satellites. A fourth satellite is then used to validate the information obtained from the other three. This additional satellite enables GPS to provide altitude information, thus moving us into the third dimension. GPS operates using a technique known as trilateration or triangulation. Trilateration utilizes signals to calculate location, velocity, and elevation, while triangulation is employed to measure angles rather than distances. Satellites transmit signals to GPS devices on or near the Earth's surface, and a device must be capable of receiving signals from at least four satellites to calculate its location. Each satellite orbits the Earth twice a day, transmitting a unique signal along with orbital parameters and time information. A GPS system can receive signals from six or more satellites. A GPS device captures microwave signals from satellites to determine the distance between the satellite and the GPS system. However, since GPS provides only distance information, it alone cannot provide precise location data. A single satellite sends a signal, creating a circle. The second satellite creates another circle, narrowing down the location to one of two points where the circles intersect. With the third satellite, the location is determined as the device lies at the intersection point of the three circles. However, our world is three-dimensional in nature. Satellites generate spheres instead of circles, resulting in two points of intersection for the three spheres from the three satellites. Finally, the point nearest to the Earth's surface is chosen as the location.

As GPS moves, the radius, which is the distance from the two satellites, changes, thereby generating new spheres that provide updated positions.

GPS operates continuously, regardless of weather conditions. Hence, it is a powerful and dependable tool in various industries and other areas of business and organizations. Pilots, boat captains, surveyors, scientists, and workers rely on GPS information in their daily work. It is used for preparing accurate surveys and maps, conducting precise time measurements, and tracking positions or locations Uses of GPS: i) Location findings ii) Navigation ( or finding of another location from a given location) iii) Tracking ( For an object's or a person's movement) iv) Mapping of the world. v) Timing for the precise measurement Factors Affecting GPS Accuracy:

Following are the key factors that affect the GPS accuracy: i) Atmospheric conditions: solar storms, heavy storm cover and ionospheric delays disturb the GPS system. ii) Physical conditions: High altitude mountainous regions, trees and tall buildings disturb the signals passage time. iii) Calculation Error: It occurs from the device’s hardware. iv) Ephemeris: It occurs due to the incorrect orbital model within the satellite.
Components of GPS System: It consists of mainly three segments:

Space (satellite segment): The 24-satellite orbiting twice a day transmit signals to users on the Earth with timing. Control Segment: It includes tracking and operating the satellite in space and monitoring transmissions. For this, 5 monitoring stations are kept almost in all the continent with North and South America combined. Qualified signals are sent to the master control stations. In case of defects in signals, hey are sent back to the GPS satellite. FIG User equipment (user segment); GPS receivers and transmitters collect and process signals from the GPS satellites and determine distance. The measurement accuracy increases with the number of satellites.

GPS vs GNSS; The Difference: GPS is one of several satellite constellations, while GNSS describes all satellite constellations in orbit. GNSS is formed by combining multiple constellations. The accuracy of positioning technology depends on these various constellations.
